newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Waigel tax reforms clear Bundestag hurdle.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Waigel tax reforms clear Bundestag hurdle.

text.p: Finance Minister Theo Waigel's tax-cutting reforms cleared the German lower house of parliament on Thursday, but the bills angered business groups and face rejection in the opposition-controlled upper house.

The 1998 and 1999 tax bills, which envisage net tax cuts of 30 billion marks ($17.4 billion), were passed comfortably in the Bundestag with the backing of deputies from Chancellor Helmut Kohl's three-party coalition.
Waigel told the chamber that the reforms would meet the challenge of globalisation by attracting investment and creating new jobs in an economy plagued by unemployment.
Big income and corporate tax cuts in the next two years would actually revive failing state revenues by boosting economic growth and closing ways to avoid paying tax.
"I am convinced...that such a structural change in the tax system and a cut in tax rates would not lead to a fall in tax revenues, but a stabilisation and a long-term rise," he said.
The reform, which was amended in committee, would cut the lowest rate of income tax to 15 percent in 1999 from 39 percent while the top rate would fall to 39 percent from 53.

The solidarity income tax surcharge, raised to help rebuild ex-communist eastern Germany, would fall by two percentage points to 5.5 percent next year. The top rate of corporation tax would fall in two steps to 35 percent by 1999 from 45 percent now.

Opposition speakers attacked the financing of the reforms, which they said would leave a budget gap of 45 billion marks. To close the gap Waigel would have to announce a rise in value-added tax after next year's general election, they said.

"The government's policy will neither revive the economy nor create jobs -- it is the writing on the wall for doing business in Germany and for the welfare state," said Christine Scheel, finance spokeswoman for the opposition Greens party.
Opposition Social Democrat (SPD) parliamentary chief Rudolf Scharping said: "This is a deceitful tax reform, and it will not get the support of the SPD."

Without referring to tough borrowing targets for the planned European single currency, Waigel said he was seeking more budget savings to make room for tax cuts. The cabinet is due to sign off on the 1998 budget on July 11.

The reforms limit company writeoffs against losses and tax reserves built up by utilities to shut down nuclear power plants. The Bundestag also called on the government to look into tax breaks on taking over lossmaking firms.

The Federation of German Industry (BDI), whose president Hans-Olaf Henkel has described the amended reforms as a scandal, said Waigel's forecast for new investment and jobs was wrong. "Instead of bringing vital relief to industry, the tax burden will rise," the BDI said in a statement.
"The latest decision to limit writing off tax against losses will make it difficult, if not impossible, for companies to cope. This must have a negative impact on investment."
The tax bills now move on for review by the SPD-controlled upper house, the Bundesrat, on July 4. The SPD said it would reject the measures, landing them in parliament's mediation process.
Kohl, who did not take part in the tax debate, said earlier that he still expected to reach agreement with the SPD on tax by the autumn in the mediation committee.

"We'll talk and then in the autumn there will be a tax reform," Kohl told SAT1 television in an interview. "It will not be identical to the tax reform we adopt today -- that belongs to the way parliamentary mediation works. But there will be significant progress. There will be a tax cut."

In stark contrast to the confrontational tax debate, the SPD backed the Kohl coalition in passing Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt's bill to secure state aid to eastern Germany after the current funding plan runs out in 1998.

According to the bill, 5.7 billion marks a year will be granted from 1999 onwards in the form of investment bonuses for companies. "The east German economy, which is already doing better, will thus gain extra momentum," Rexrodt said. ($ = 1.725 German Marks)
